# SMSD <img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="right" height="139" alt="SMSD hex logo" />

SMSD (Sequential Methods for Study Design) is for researchers who have to
plan a study without knowing the population values that a sample size
formula asks for: a standard deviation, a correlation, or the effect size
itself. A sequential procedure does not guess them. Data are collected in
stages, and after each stage a stopping rule computed from the data in hand
says whether the goal has been reached. The goal can be a confidence
interval as narrow as requested (accuracy in parameter estimation, AIPE),
an estimate whose combined cost of estimation error and of sampling is as
small as it can be made (minimum risk point estimation, MRPE), or the most
precise estimate of a contrast that a fixed budget can buy. The methods are
general; the articles that developed them have psychology, education,
management, and related fields in view. The confidence interval procedures
for effect sizes assume no particular distribution for the data, with the
exception of the one for the squared multiple correlation.

## Installation

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
# The released version, from CRAN
install.packages("SMSD")

# Or the development version, from GitHub (one of the two, not both)
# install.packages("remotes")
# remotes::install_github("yelleKneK/SMSD")
```

Install the source tarball identified by the release record when you need
this exact version. A CRAN mirror or the public GitHub branch can serve a
different version, so verify `packageVersion("SMSD")` after installation.
The tarball can be installed with `install.packages("SMSD_1.0.0.tar.gz",
repos = NULL, type = "source")`; install its required dependencies first.
The package needs DMAR 1.0.0 or later and R 4.0.0 or later.

For the replication of published examples, see
`vignette("published-examples", package = "SMSD")`. For measured coverage,
sample sizes, and figures from difficult designs, see
`vignette("coverage-and-design", package = "SMSD")`.

## Where to Start

Start with `seq_aipe_smd()`, the standardized mean difference between two
groups. Suppose a training program is compared with a control condition on
employee engagement, and the aim is a 95% confidence interval for the
standardized mean difference that is no wider than 0.60. The pilot function
gives the first sample size, and the check function says whether sampling
can stop. (The data are simulated, with a true difference of 0.4 standard
deviations, so that the example runs on its own.)

```{r start, message = FALSE}
library(SMSD)
set.seed(113)
trained <- rnorm(seq_aipe_smd_pilot(width = 0.60), mean = 4.9)
control <- rnorm(seq_aipe_smd_pilot(width = 0.60), mean = 4.5)
seq_aipe_smd(trained, control, width = 0.60)
```

```{r start-facts, include = FALSE}
first <- seq_aipe_smd(trained, control, width = 0.60)
stopifnot(!attr(first, "is_satisfied"))
```

With the pilot sample of `r length(trained)` people per group the rule is
not met: the criterion asks for `r attr(first, "criterion_n")` per group as
things stand, and that number is updated at every check. A study therefore
adds participants and checks again, until the rule is met. `seq_report()`
then writes the result up.

```{r continue}
out <- seq_aipe_smd(trained, control, width = 0.60)
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  trained <- c(trained, rnorm(1, mean = 4.9))
  control <- c(control, rnorm(1, mean = 4.5))
  out <- seq_aipe_smd(trained, control, width = 0.60)
}
seq_report(out)
```

```{r continue-facts, include = FALSE}
limits <- out$value[out$term %in% c("lower_limit", "upper_limit")]
stopifnot(attr(out, "is_satisfied"), diff(limits) <= 0.60,
          limits[1] < 0.4, 0.4 < limits[2])
```

The final interval is `r sprintf("%.3f", diff(limits))` wide (computed
from the limits before they are rounded for the report), within the 0.60
requested, and it contains the 0.4 used to generate the data. The check
function does not prompt and keeps nothing between calls: the loop belongs
to the study, and each call is a calculation on the data collected so far. For data already in hand, `seq_path()` runs the same loop in one
call and `plot()` draws it. `vignette("introduction", package = "SMSD")` is
the overview, and `vignette("step-by-step-sequential-workflow", package =
"SMSD")` follows one study from its pilot sample to its stopping point.

## Which Function Do I Need?

```{r table-facts, include = FALSE}
exports <- getNamespaceExports("SMSD")
pilots <- grep("_pilot$", exports, value = TRUE)
sensitivity <- grep("_sensitivity$", exports, value = TRUE)
checks <- sub("_pilot$", "", pilots)
stopifnot(all(checks %in% exports))
```

| What you want | Function | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **A Narrow Confidence Interval for an Effect Size** | | |
| Standardized mean difference | `seq_aipe_smd()` | Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay (2018) |
| Pearson, Kendall, or Spearman correlation | `seq_aipe_r()` | Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay (2019) |
| Squared multiple correlation (multivariate normal data) | `seq_aipe_R2()` | Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay (2019) |
| Coefficient of variation | `seq_aipe_cv()` | Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay (2018) |
| Simple linear regression slope | `seq_aipe_reg_coef()` | Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay (2018) |
| Standardized mean | `seq_aipe_sm()` | Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay (2018) |
| Contrast of group means | `seq_aipe_c()` | Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay (2018) |
| Gini index | `seq_aipe_gini()` | Chattopadhyay & De (2016) |
| **Minimum Risk Point Estimation** (the smallest combined cost of error and of sampling) | | |
| Coefficient of variation | `seq_mr_cv()` | Chattopadhyay & Kelley (2016) |
| Standardized mean difference, with one sampling cost or one per group | `seq_mr_smd()` | Chattopadhyay & Kelley (2017) |
| **A Budget Across Groups** | | |
| The check, and the group to sample next | `seq_budget()`, `seq_budget_next()` | Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, & Padalunkal (2025) |
| The allocation if the standard deviations were known | `seq_budget_optimal()` | Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, & Padalunkal (2025) |
| A noninferiority, superiority, inferiority, or equivalence decision | `decide_seq_budget_noninferiority()`, `decide_seq_budget_superiority()`, `decide_seq_budget_inferiority()`, `decide_seq_budget_equivalence()` | Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, & Padalunkal (2025) |
| **Classical Procedures for a Mean, a Median, or a Location** | | |
| A fixed width interval for a mean | `seq_fwd_norm_mean()`, `seq_fwd_dfr_mean()`; in two stages, `ts_fwd_norm_mean()`, `ts_fwd_dfr_mean()` | Mukhopadhyay & de Silva (2009) |
| The location of a negative exponential distribution | `seq_fwd_nexp_mean()`, `ts_fwd_nexp_mean()`, `seq_mr_nexp_mean()` | Mukhopadhyay & de Silva (2009) |
| An interval of bounded length for a median | `seq_blci_dfr_median()` | Mukhopadhyay & de Silva (2009) |
| A mean estimated with bounded risk | `seq_br_norm_mean()`; in two stages, `ts_br_norm_mean()`, `ts_br_exp_mean()` | Mukhopadhyay & de Silva (2009) |
| A mean estimated with minimum risk | `seq_mr_norm_mean()`, `seq_mr_exp_mean()`, `seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb()` | Mukhopadhyay & de Silva (2009) |
| **Studying a Design Before Collecting Data** | | |
| The final sample size, interval width, and coverage to expect | `seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity()` and its siblings for every `seq_aipe_*` function | The article of the procedure simulated |
| The final sample size and risk to expect | `seq_mr_cv_sensitivity()`, `seq_mr_smd_sensitivity()` | The article of the procedure simulated |
| The cost, coverage, and decisions to expect under a budget | `seq_budget_sensitivity()` | Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, & Padalunkal (2025) |
| **Reading and Reporting a Result** | | |
| The result of one check | `print()`, `summary()`, `generics::tidy()`, `generics::glance()` | This package |
| The whole stopping path for data in hand, and its picture | `seq_path()`, `plot()` | This package |
| A paragraph for the methods or results section | `seq_report()` | This package; the paragraph cites the article of the procedure |

Each of the `r length(checks)` check functions has a companion that returns
its pilot sample size and is named by adding `_pilot`, as in
`seq_aipe_smd_pilot()`. In all, the package exports `r length(exports)`
functions, `r length(sensitivity)` of them `_sensitivity()` functions.
`help("SMSD-package")` lists every one of them with a link.

The `seq_aipe_*` functions take the full width of the interval as `width`.
The classical interval procedures take `d`, and what `d` measures depends on
the procedure: the half width of the interval for a mean
(`seq_fwd_norm_mean()`, `seq_fwd_dfr_mean()`, `ts_fwd_norm_mean()`,
`ts_fwd_dfr_mean()`), the full width for the location of a negative
exponential distribution (`seq_fwd_nexp_mean()`, `ts_fwd_nexp_mean()`), and
half of the largest length allowed for the interval for a median
(`seq_blci_dfr_median()`). Likewise `gamma` has two meanings. In
`seq_mr_cv()`, `seq_mr_smd()`, `seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb()`, and their pilot
functions it is the exponent of the correction term
*n*<sup>−γ</sup> in the stopping rule; in the other pilot functions of the
classical procedures it is a constant of the pilot rule that sets the size
of the pilot sample. Each help page says which.

## What the Procedures Guarantee

The `seq_aipe_*` procedures deliver the requested width by construction:
when the stopping rule is met, the interval is no wider than the target.
Coverage is a different matter. It is an asymptotic property, reached as
the target narrows and the final sample grows, and it can fall well short
of the confidence level in the small samples that a wide target, a strong
relationship, or many predictors produce. The sensitivity functions show
what to expect before any data are collected. Each row below is one call.

```{r guarantee}
G <- 2000
runs <- list(
  "Standardized mean difference of 0.5, width 0.8" =
    seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity(0.5, width = 0.8, G = G, seed = 113),
  "Pearson correlation of 0.4, width 0.4" =
    seq_aipe_r_sensitivity(0.4, width = 0.4, G = G, seed = 113),
  "Pearson correlation of 0.8, width 0.4" =
    seq_aipe_r_sensitivity(0.8, width = 0.4, G = G, seed = 113),
  "Regression slope of 0.5, width 0.4" =
    seq_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity(0.5, width = 0.4, G = G, seed = 113),
  "Coefficient of variation of 0.5, lognormal data, width 0.2" =
    seq_aipe_cv_sensitivity(0.5, width = 0.2, distribution = "lognormal",
                            G = G, seed = 113),
  "Squared multiple correlation of 0.5, 5 predictors, width 0.3" =
    seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity(0.5, width = 0.3, p = 5, G = G, seed = 113),
  "Squared multiple correlation of 0.5, 15 predictors, width 0.3" =
    seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity(0.5, width = 0.3, p = 15, G = G, seed = 113)
)
row_of <- function(term) vapply(runs, function(run) run$value[run$term == term], 0)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(names(runs), row_of("mean_n"), row_of("pct_width_within"),
             row_of("coverage")),
  digits = c(0, 0, 0, 2), row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Design", "Mean final sample size",
                "Intervals within the width (%)", "Coverage of the 95% interval")
)
```

```{r guarantee-facts, include = FALSE}
coverage <- row_of("coverage")
se <- sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / G)
strong <- grep("correlation of 0.8", names(runs))
weak <- grep("correlation of 0.4", names(runs))
stopifnot(all(row_of("pct_width_within") == 100), all(row_of("pct_hit_max_n") == 0),
          abs(coverage[1] - 0.95) < 3 * se[1], all(coverage[-1] < 0.90),
          which.min(coverage) == length(coverage),
          grepl("15 predictors", names(runs)[length(runs)]),
          length(strong) == 1, length(weak) == 1,
          coverage[strong] < coverage[weak])
two <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
# The sentences below quote the table, so the two ways of rounding must agree.
stopifnot(identical(two(coverage), format(round(unname(coverage), 2), nsmall = 2)))
```

Every interval in every row was within its target width. Coverage was close
to the nominal level for the standardized mean difference
(`r two(coverage[1])`, with a Monte Carlo standard error of
`r sprintf("%.3f", se[1])`) and well below it in the other rows, from
`r two(max(coverage[-1]))` down to
`r two(min(coverage[-1]))` for the squared multiple correlation with 15
predictors. For the Pearson correlation it was lower for the strong
relationship (`r two(coverage[strong])`) than for the moderate one
(`r two(coverage[weak])`). Each figure comes from
`r format(G, big.mark = ",")` simulated studies and has a Monte Carlo
standard error of at most `r sprintf("%.3f", max(se))`, so another run of
the same design, such as the one a help page reports, can differ from it in
the second decimal. (The sample sizes count observations per group for the
standardized mean difference, pairs for the correlation and the slope, and
observations otherwise.) A narrower target, which means a larger study,
brings coverage toward the nominal level; a larger minimum pilot sample
(`m_0`) helps as well. The help page of each `seq_aipe_*` function states
what its guarantee is and reports what was measured for it, and
`?seq_aipe_sensitivity` has a table over more conditions.

In a small sample the variance estimate that a stopping rule needs can be
zero, negative, or not finite. The check functions then report the rule as
not met, with a note, and sampling continues. This is a deliberate departure
from the rules as printed in the articles, under which the study would stop
at once with an interval far narrower than requested; the section "An
Unusable Variance Estimate" of `help("SMSD-package")` describes it.

The classical procedures state their guarantees on their help pages as well.
Some are exact: Stein's two stage interval, `ts_fwd_norm_mean()`, covers a
normal mean with at least the stated probability for any first stage. Others
are asymptotic: the distribution free two stage interval,
`ts_fwd_dfr_mean()`, covers a normal mean with probability
`r sprintf("%.3f", 2 * pt(qnorm(0.975), df = 29) - 1)` at a nominal 0.95 when
the first stage has 30 observations and the target is narrow, and with less
for skewed data.

## Validation

```{r validation-facts, include = FALSE}
study <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "aipe_simulation_results.rds",
                             package = "SMSD"))
conditions <- nrow(study$summary)
replications <- unique(study$summary$G)
stopifnot(is.data.frame(study$summary), conditions > 0,
          length(replications) == 1, replications >= 1000)
test_files <- length(list.files("tests/testthat", pattern = "^test-.*[.]R$"))
stopifnot(test_files > 0,
          nzchar(system.file("eq26_correction.pdf", package = "SMSD")),
          nzchar(system.file("cv_variance_note.md", package = "SMSD")))
```

* **Tests that pin published values.** The test suite (`r test_files` test
  files) compares the package with numbers printed in the source articles:
  rows of Tables 2, 3, and 4 of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018);
  rows of Tables 2, 10, 11, 13, and 14 of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay
  (2019); the worked examples and rows of Table 1 of Chattopadhyay and
  Kelley (2016) and of Table 3 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017); and the
  allocation example and Table 1 of Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley,
  and Padalunkal (2025). One published row is not reproduced in full, and
  its test records the difference: for Kendall's tau (Table 8 of the 2019
  article) coverage and interval width are close to the article's, but the
  mean final sample size runs about 2 percent above the published one and
  varies nearly twice as much from study to study. The cause is not
  resolved. Where no table exists, a procedure is run to its stopping point
  and compared with its theoretical sample size or its exact guarantee.
* **A cached simulation study.** A study of the standardized mean difference
  and Pearson correlation procedures under normal and skewed data
  (`r conditions` conditions, `r format(replications, big.mark = ",")`
  replications each) is installed with the package, at
  `system.file("extdata", "aipe_simulation_results.rds", package = "SMSD")`,
  and is displayed and discussed in `vignette("complete-tour", package =
  "SMSD")`. The script that produces it is in the `data-raw` folder of the
  source repository.
* **Two notes on departures from the articles as printed.** The variance of
  the standardized mean difference corrects an omitted factor of 1/2 in
  Equation 26 of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018). The correction is
  installed with the package
  (`system.file("eq26_correction.pdf", package = "SMSD")`) and is posted by
  the authors at
  <https://kenkelley.org/wp-content/uploads/articles/Kelley_Darku_Chattopadhyay_Equation_26.pdf>.
  In `seq_mr_cv()` the variance of the coefficient of variation is by
  default the estimator of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018), which is
  consistent for any distribution with a finite fourth moment. Equation 22
  of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016) agrees with it for normal data, and
  for any population with no excess kurtosis, and can differ otherwise;
  `variance = "published"` uses that equation, so that the article can be
  reproduced. The derivation is in a note installed with the package
  (`system.file("cv_variance_note.md", package = "SMSD")`), and `?seq_mr_cv`
  summarizes it.
* **A comparison with the published tables.** The validation article of the
  package website (`vignettes/articles/validation.Rmd` in the source
  repository) sets the package's results beside the published ones, table
  by table.

## How to Cite

```{r cite-facts, include = FALSE}
entries <- utils::readCitationFile("inst/CITATION",
                                   meta = as.list(description[1, ]))
articles <- sum(vapply(entries, function(entry) entry$bibtype == "Article", NA))
stopifnot(articles == length(entries) - 1, articles >= 1, articles <= 9)
in_words <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight",
              "nine")
```

`citation("SMSD")` gives the package entry and the `r in_words[articles]`
articles listed here, and `toBibtex(citation("SMSD"))` gives them as BibTeX
entries.
Please cite the package and the article that developed the method you used.
The book is the source of the classical procedures.

* Chattopadhyay, B., Bandyopadhyay, T., Kelley, K., & Padalunkal, J. J.
  (2025). A sequential approach for noninferiority or equivalence of a
  linear contrast under cost constraints. *Psychological Methods, 30*(2),
  425--439. [doi:10.1037/met0000570](https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000570)
* Chattopadhyay, B., & De, S. K. (2016). Estimation of Gini index within
  pre-specified error bound. *Econometrics, 4*(3), 30.
  [doi:10.3390/econometrics4030030](https://doi.org/10.3390/econometrics4030030)
* Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient of
  variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing sampling
  error and study cost. *Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51*(5), 627--648.
  [doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279](https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279)
* Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2017). Estimating the standardized mean
  difference with minimum risk: Maximizing accuracy and minimizing cost with
  sequential estimation. *Psychological Methods, 22*(1), 94--113.
  [doi:10.1037/met0000089](https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000089)
* Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in
  parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential
  approach. *Psychological Methods, 23*(2), 226--243.
  [doi:10.1037/met0000127](https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000127)
* Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2019). Sequential accuracy
  in parameter estimation for population correlation coefficients.
  *Psychological Methods, 24*(4), 492--515.
  [doi:10.1037/met0000203](https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000203)
* Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). *Sequential methods and their
  applications*. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN\:9780367386535
